title: Mahjong Leagues for Senior Living Communities
one_liner: A turnkey mahjong program (kits, instructors, scoring app, inter-community leagues) sold to senior-living activity directors.
customer: Activity directors at independent and assisted living communities (roughly 30k in the US), 55+ HOAs, and library systems.
problem: Mahjong is booming: CNN (19 Sept 2026) covers the explosion, Yelp searches for mahjong clubs rose about 4,467% in 2025, and the National Mah Jongg League reports 350k+ members. Coverage frames it as a Gen Z and millennial aesthetic trend. Meanwhile senior-living calendars need social, cognitive, low-injury weekly activities, and American mahjong is hard to learn and hard to staff with teachers.
solution: A subscription with a 4-table starter kit, certified instructor visits (in person or video), monthly inter-community league nights with a shared leaderboard and trophy, a coordinator app, and staff training so the community can run it alone.
why_now: The mainstream boom is producing demand and a supply of instructors from the new club scene. Pickleball injuries make low-impact alternatives attractive for the same age group.
revenue_model: $300-600/month per community, $250 kits, per-visit instructor fees, and tile-maker sponsorships.
non_obvious_insight: Tile brands and influencers chase young buyers with $200 designer sets. The recurring money sits with older players who play weekly and with institutions that have a budget line called 'activities'. Inter-facility leagues create retention and sales compounding, because a community that joins forces its rivals to join.
first_30_days: Approach 20 senior communities in one metro via activity-director networks. Run free two-week pilots staffed by 2 volunteer instructors recruited from local clubs. Convert 5 into $300/month accounts and stage the first inter-community match.

title: Do-Not-Clone Voice Registry With Inference-Time Checks
one_liner: A privacy-preserving registry that voice-cloning vendors query before creating a clone, so voice actors and narrators can block or price unauthorized cloning at the moment of input.
customer: Voice actors, audiobook narrators and podcasters (and their agents) as enrolled voices, and TTS, dubbing, audiobook and podcast-tool vendors that pay for checks and compliance logs.
problem: YouTube's likeness detection is gated by agencies and celebrity status, with no path for long-tail creators, and its removals so far are 'very small.' State laws such as Tennessee's ELVIS Act and California's digital-replica statutes create liability for cloning without consent. Vendors want a cheap way to show good faith. Detection after distribution is a losing race.
solution: Enrolled voices are stored as one-way speaker-embedding hashes. Vendors call a check API with the reference clip before creating a clone. A match requires a proof-of-consent token that carries the owner's terms (price, banned categories). Owners get logs and payouts via vendor marketplaces. Start with voice actors enrolled through agents and narrators' communities, integrated with 2-3 mid-size TTS or dubbing vendors.
why_now: Likeness laws now exist in several places, the gap for non-celebrity creators is visible, speaker-embedding models are open, and vendors selling to enterprises need a compliance line item.
revenue_model: $0.002-0.01 per check plus $1-5k/month compliance tiers for vendors, per-talent annual fees from agencies, and a marketplace take rate.
non_obvious_insight: The money is on the liability side (vendors), not the creator side, and enforcement is cheapest at input (before a clone exists) rather than at output, where the detection war is being lost.
first_30_days: Build the registry and check API prototype. Enroll 100 voice actors through two agents and a narrators' Discord. Trial the check API free with five TTS and dubbing startups, aiming for a first paid compliance tier from a dubbing vendor.

title: Settlement Passports for Florida High-Rise Condos
one_liner: A satellite-radar settlement history for every Florida condo tower, sold as the cheap first page of the milestone-inspection and reserve-study file.
customer: Florida condo associations and the licensed engineers and property managers who run their milestone inspections and structural integrity reserve studies; secondary buyers are master-policy underwriters, lenders and buyers' agents doing condo diligence.
problem: Carriers want structural documents before they bind a master policy, SIRS and milestone inspections are mandatory for 3+ story buildings, and special assessments run $50K-$200K+ per unit. Boards cannot tell whether their building is stable or sinking until an engineer bills for scoping. A 2024 University of Miami InSAR study found 35 Miami Beach to Sunny Isles buildings subsiding 2-8 cm over 2016-2023, and no commercial product packages this for boards.
solution: Process free Sentinel-1 radar (2015 onward), ESA archive radar for the 1990s-2010s, and newly public NISAR L-band data into a per-building vertical-motion trend. Add differential tilt across the footprint and a comparison against neighbours built on similar fill. Deliver a 3-page Settlement Passport plus a monitoring feed, positioned as a screening indicator that sharpens inspection scope, with an engineer partner signing off. It is not a substitute for the inspection.
why_now: Florida's post-Surfside SB 4-D inspection and reserve-study mandates are now enforced and carriers demand documents. NISAR L-band data has been free through ASF since the July 20, 2026 public release, adding to the Sentinel-1 record. Peer-reviewed proof that InSAR resolves individual Miami towers exists but has not been productized. Reinsurance is softening while condo retail insurance is still squeezed.
revenue_model: $900-$2,500 per building for the initial passport and $300/yr for monitoring. Wholesale price of about $400 to engineering firms who bundle it into SIRS work. $100/building/yr portfolio contracts for management companies.
non_obvious_insight: InSAR is treated as an academic or pipeline-monitoring tool, but the buyer with a legal deadline and a real budget is a condo board that must assemble a structural file. Persistent-scatterer InSAR works best on concrete high-rises, the exact asset at issue. The 10-30 year archive can also show a building has been stable for decades, which makes it a positive underwriting asset for the many buildings that are fine, not just a warning label.
first_30_days: Run the free Sentinel-1 stack for about 400 buildings on the Miami-Dade and Broward barrier islands. Offer one free passport to each of 15 engineering firms and 5 management companies, and sign 2 engineers as resellers. Then charge the first 10 boards facing reserve-study or insurance-renewal deadlines.

title: Spindle-Hour Options: Reserve Capacity, Skip Inventory
one_liner: Standardized capacity-reservation contracts that let OEMs hedge supply risk by paying a small premium for guaranteed machining hours.
customer: Procurement leads at $50M-$1B OEMs (industrial equipment, medical devices, defense subcontractors) and 10-100 person job shops with idle spindles.
problem: 57% of negative ISM comments cite price volatility, and one respondent called lead times worse than the pandemic era. Machine-shop owners report buying a full year of inventory to lock in prices. That ties up cash and risks obsolescence. Marketplaces sell only spot capacity, and shops cannot get predictable base load.
solution: A standard reservation contract by machine class (3-axis, 5-axis, Swiss, wire EDM, weld cell). The buyer pays a reservation fee for N hours a month over 6-12 months at a strike rate, with materials indexed to published metals prices. The buyer exercises by releasing drawings within 10 days. The platform vets shops, holds deposits in escrow, and resells unexercised hours to spot buyers.
why_now: Metals repricing under Section 232, Hormuz freight shocks, machinery hiring picking up, and auto-supplier capacity going idle. Buyers can no longer count on spot capacity appearing.
revenue_model: 6-10% of reservation fees plus 2-3% of exercised work. Later, underwrite a portfolio of options for the spread.
non_obvious_insight: A job shop's most valuable asset is certainty of base load, and it will discount 10-20% for take-or-pay. Buyers fear not getting parts more than they fear price. An option on capacity is a cheaper hedge than a year of inventory, and the deposit doubles as working capital for the shop.
first_30_days: Recruit 8-10 shops with one machine class in one region (for example Northeast Ohio). Draft a two-page contract with a manufacturing lawyer. Pitch 15 buyers who are already stockpiling inventory. Aim for $50k in reservations by day 60. Run it as a brokerage first.

title: Powered Public Land Brokerage for Robotaxi Depots
one_liner: A broker that matches autonomous-fleet operators to cities' already-energized, under-used land such as transit depots, fleet yards and city garages, on leases that trade concessions cities value.
customer: Robotaxi, autonomous delivery-van and driverless-truck operators pay success fees and retainers (Waymo, Zoox, May Mobility, Avride, Gatik and others). Cities and transit agencies are the counterparty, earning lease income.
problem: Depot power is the choke point for scaling robotaxis. A standard California charging site takes about 6 months, a new circuit 1.9 years, a substation upgrade 2.8 years and a new substation 8.9 years, and depots now compete with data centers for powered industrial land. Waymo's first 86M miles were only 54% passenger-carrying, so depots and reset cycles matter more than vehicles. AV operators do not know which public parcels are already energized, because they sit in transit-agency asset registers rather than commercial real estate databases.
solution: Build a dataset of municipally owned parcels with existing high-capacity service: bus depots, municipal fleet yards, park-and-ride lots, closed school-bus yards, airport lots and city garages. Overlay it with utility load-capacity maps. Use a template 'public benefit lease' (revenue share, 24/7 emergency access, data sharing, wheelchair-accessible service commitments, local cleaning and charging jobs) so cities can say yes without a full RFP. Then broker the deals.
why_now: Waymo raised $16B at a $126B valuation in Feb 2026 and is expanding across 10-14 metros. Zoox began charging fares on Aug 10, 2026, Tesla is running unsupervised in two states, and Aurora is exiting 2026 with 200 driverless trucks that need terminals. Large-load grid queues are freezing in Texas, so already-energized land is worth years.
revenue_model: A success fee of 3-5% of lease value or $75-150k per signed site, plus $10-20k/month retainers from fleets that want a standing pipeline. Optional revenue share with the city.
non_obvious_insight: The scarcest input for autonomous-fleet scale is already-energized land, not compute or vehicles, and the largest holder of it is city government. City government cannot run a competitive marketplace but values non-cash concessions (accessibility, data, jobs) that a private landlord never offers.
first_30_days: In Texas, Arizona and Georgia metros with announced AV expansions, file public-records requests for depot and yard inventories plus utility service sizes. Build a 100-parcel shortlist. Pitch three fleet real-estate leads a paid $25k 'top-10 sites' report.

title: Air-Permit Unlock for Idle Data Center Diesel
one_liner: Turn the ~55 GW of idle data center backup generators into dispatchable capacity by solving the air-permit problem instead of the hardware problem.
customer: Colo and hyperscale operators in PJM (Northern Virginia, Ohio, Illinois) with 20-500 MW of backup gensets. Secondary buyers are utilities and capacity buyers who need fast MW.
problem: Data centers hold about 55 GW of backup diesel (Virginia alone has about 27 GW permitted), and it runs 10-30 minutes a month. PJM cleared 6.8 GW short and wants large loads to bring their own capacity or be curtailed. Air permits cap non-emergency run hours, so nobody can legally count these engines as capacity.
solution: Fixed-price 'permit-to-dispatch' packages. They cover a state-specific permit modification strategy (run-hour caps, synthetic-minor limits), engineering and financing for emissions retrofits on the subset of engines that need them, and paralleling/telemetry upgrades. Enrollment in PJM's on-site backup (IRAS-style) and demand-response programs comes with third-party measurement and verification. Runtime is capped at a few dozen to ~100 hours a year, dispatched only in system emergencies, with community disclosure built in.
why_now: PJM's July auction shortfall, the proposed backstop auction (15-year terms, $555/MW-day cap) and the curtailment-or-bring-capacity rule make backup generation valuable for the first time. Turbines are sold out until 2029-30, so this fleet is the only large block of capacity that exists today.
revenue_model: $40-150k fixed fee per site for permit and engineering work, plus 10-20% of the first five years of capacity revenue. At the $325/MW-day cap a 20 MW fleet is worth very roughly $1.5-2M a year after derating, so the fee is easy to justify. Retrofit financing adds a spread.
non_obvious_insight: The cheapest big block of new PJM capacity is not new. It is already built and sitting behind a fence, and the barrier is air-permit lawyering that VC-backed hardware companies ignore. A repeatable per-state permit playbook is the moat. Emergency-only runtime is why it works: at under 1% of hours, the capacity value dwarfs the emissions.
first_30_days: Pull public Title V and minor-source permit files for ~30 colo sites in VA, OH and IL. Build a 'permit headroom map' showing run-hour caps and engine tiers. Retain one air-permitting consultant. Offer 25 facility and sustainability leads a $15k fixed-fee dispatch-readiness audit of a 20+ MW fleet and aim to close two paid pilots.

title: Roof Rebuttal Kits for Aerial-Photo Insurance Drops
one_liner: A 48-hour, flat-fee evidence packet and cheap-fix dispatch that lets homeowners beat insurer non-renewals based on aerial imagery instead of paying $20k for an unneeded roof.
customer: Homeowners who receive a non-renewal or 'replace your roof in 30-60 days' letter (paying $249-$399 flat). The hidden second buyer is independent insurance agents, who lose the commission when a policy leaves and would pay a white-label subscription.
problem: Carriers and their imagery vendors (State Farm reportedly uses CAPE Analytics and Nearmap) flag moss, algae, skylights, solar panels, tree overhang, pools or trampolines from aerial photos. Homeowners get a short cure window, are told to replace a roof (one Santa Ana homeowner was quoted about $20,000 with a May 1 deadline and could not find replacement coverage), and are often refused the images. In one Galveston case the roofer said the roof only needed a thorough cleaning, yet the insurer would not share its report or photos.
solution: Local dispatch of a licensed roof inspector or drone pilot who produces an insurer-formatted rebuttal packet: dated, geotagged photos, remaining-life certification, an overlay labeling the skylight, solar panel or moss that the insurer's image mislabeled, and a written cure quote. Where a real defect exists, a vetted soft-wash or repair contractor does the cheap cure (hundreds of dollars, not replacement). The kit also includes a request-the-images letter, a state Department of Insurance complaint draft, and a re-shop packet showing roof condition to alternative carriers.
why_now: Aerial and AI underwriting went mainstream in 2024-2026. DroneXL (Mar 2026) reports imagery-driven drops nationwide and that Texas non-renewals nearly doubled from 2020 to 2023. California proposed insurer-notification rules in 2025, and Massachusetts proposed a right to view the images. Consumers now need a fast, standard counter-evidence format, and cheap drones and inspection apps make a 48-hour turnaround affordable.
revenue_model: $249-$399 per packet, plus a 10-20% referral fee from cleaning and roofing contractors on cure jobs, plus a $99-$199/month white-label plan for independent agents who send at-risk clients.
non_obvious_insight: The fight is an evidence-format problem, not an insurance problem, and the cure often costs 2-5% of the replacement. A San Francisco couple insured for about 50 years had a Liberty Mutual non-renewal reversed within an hour of media pressure after a licensed roofer's written, photographed inspection showed about 20 years of remaining life (https://www.aol.com/finance/insurer-dropped-san-francisco-homeowners-131500464.html). Most homeowners cannot get that leverage. DroneXL documents the $20k quote, the Galveston 'cleaning only' case, and the vendor names (https://dronexl.co/2026/03/11/insurance-drone-roof-inspections/). United Policyholders confirms that correcting misidentifications with photos works and that only about 30 days' notice is typical (https://uphelp.org/aerial-photos-are-leading-to-insurance-non-renewals/). Reddit itself was unreachable from this environment, so this demand evidence comes from press and advocate sources describing the same recurring r/homeowners situation.
first_30_days: Pick one metro with heavy non-renewals (Houston/Galveston, the Bay Area, or the Colorado Front Range). Sign two soft-wash companies and one roof inspector with a drone at about $150 per inspection, and build a one-page site aimed at searches like 'State Farm non-renewal roof'. Post in neighborhood groups, offer the packet to 10 independent agents, and run the first 20-30 packets at $299, tracking reversal rate to build a public success statistic.

title: Diaspora-Financed Home Batteries for Family Back Home
one_liner: Sell home battery and solar systems to migrants in the US, UK, Canada and EU as a monthly subscription that keeps the lights on for their relatives, underwritten on the sender's credit rather than the recipient's.
customer: Diaspora professionals (Nigerian, Ghanaian, Kenyan, Filipino, Nepali, Bangladeshi) who already fund fuel, diesel and generator repairs for relatives, with installers in the origin city as fulfilment partners.
problem: Families in Lagos, Accra, Nairobi or Manila face daily outages and spend remittance money on diesel and petrol for generators. Local households are unbankable for asset finance, USD lenders carry FX and default risk, and pay-as-you-go schemes collect tiny local-currency payments. The Hormuz shock has raised fuel costs and put about $50bn of Gulf remittances at risk.
solution: A subscription sold in USD, GBP or CAD. A vetted local installer fits a 5 kWh LFP battery plus hybrid inverter (and optional panels) at the relative's home, the sender pays by card over 24-36 months, and ownership transfers at the end. Underwriting uses the sender's developed-market credit profile. A shared app shows the sender live uptime and savings, and the family gets a simple power ledger. On default, the fallback is remote throttling or redeployment of the unit.
why_now: Stationary battery prices fell 45% in a year and Africa already imports more battery dollars than panels. Felix shows migrant payments can run over chat apps at $8B scale. The US 1% tax on cash-funded remittances pushes senders toward card-funded rails (buying goods and services delivered abroad is not a remittance transfer, subject to legal review), and Nigeria and Kenya are opening rules for digital-dollar settlement.
revenue_model: Hardware margin of 15-25% plus a financing spread (about 18-25% effective APR), installer referral fees, and insurance and extended-warranty attach. Dollar collections match dollar-denominated hardware and DFI debt, removing the FX mismatch.
non_obvious_insight: Credit risk is being priced on the wrong person. The one who effectively pays for the outage today is the diaspora sender, through diesel money, and that person has a credit file, a card and hard-currency income. The caregiving motive should also produce lower churn than pay-as-you-go.
first_30_days: Put up a landing page taking $500 refundable deposits through 3-5 Nigerian, Ghanaian or Kenyan diaspora WhatsApp, church and alumni groups. Contract one Lagos or Nairobi installer and ship 20 systems. Use uptime screenshots and family videos for the referral flywheel, and fund working capital from deposits plus a small angel or DFI debt line.

title: Royalty Co-op for Expert Robot Demonstrations
one_liner: A worker-owned data cooperative where master tradespeople record their skilled work and earn ongoing royalties when robot makers license the demonstrations.
customer: Payers are robot foundation-model teams and manipulation or humanoid startups that buy data. Suppliers are skilled tradespeople such as tire techs, electricians, welders and HVAC technicians.
problem: Data platforms pay flat hourly rates for average people making coffee. Robots need expert-quality demonstrations, and experts will not sell their edge for a one-time $20 an hour or train their own replacement without control and upside.
solution: Partner with a union local or trade school. Members use standardized capture kits (head and wrist cameras, gloves) with quality scoring. They get a guaranteed hourly rate, 30-50% of licensing revenue, and a veto over use cases. Buyers pay per curated dataset plus a royalty per training run.
why_now: Robot training data is the humanoid bottleneck. XDOF reached about $50M annualized revenue within three months of stealth, and Mecka projects $100M ARR by end-2026 on a roughly $500M valuation. Willingness to pay is proven, while worker anxiety about being trained out of a job is rising.
revenue_model: $50-500k per dataset license, with a 20-30% cooperative fee on royalties and licensing.
non_obvious_insight: Data quality follows expert willingness, and willingness follows ownership. A cooperative with collective pricing power is a supply moat that flat-wage crowd platforms cannot copy, and it turns worker fear into the product's selling point.
first_30_days: Partner with one trade school and one union local in tire and auto service or EV-charger installation. Recruit 20 masters and capture 200 hours of one task family. Sell a pilot dataset to 2 robotics startups at $30-80k.

title: Royalty-Paying Archive of Master Tradespeople's Hands
one_liner: Pay retiring master electricians, pipefitters and welders to record expert egocentric video with think-aloud narration, license it to robotics companies, and share royalties with the workers.
customer: Robotics and embodied-AI companies building construction, maintenance and data center installation robots, and foundation-model labs. A second buyer is apprenticeship programs and trade schools, which can license the annotated footage as curriculum.
problem: Egocentric data for robots is being commoditized at the bottom: in September 2026 reporting, gig workers earn about $3-10 an hour filming dishwashing and folding laundry. Expert tasks, like reading a bad splice or feeling a torque, are rare in the data, and the people who know them are retiring, which is also the labor shortage the AI buildout depends on.
solution: Recruit 60+ year-old tradespeople through union retiree halls. Pay $60-120 an hour to wear head and wrist cameras (plus IMU gloves) on real jobs with owner consent, and to narrate why they choose each action and how they detect problems. Add edge-case tagging by a second expert. Blur faces and PII. License datasets by the hour, and pay each worker a royalty of 10-20% of license revenue and a residual on repeat licensing.
why_now: In 2026 papers such as EgoHumanoid showed that robot-free human egocentric demonstrations can train humanoid manipulation directly, so human video is now a working input. The commodity layer is crowded and cheap, so expert-conditioned data is the next premium. Labor and IP disputes over gig data are also starting, which makes a royalty model a moat.
revenue_model: License $150-600 per hour of expert-annotated footage (a hypothesis to test in pilots), exclusivity premiums, and pre-paid data collection contracts. Secondary revenue from trade-school curriculum licenses.
non_obvious_insight: Robotics' bottleneck is shifting from quantity to tacit expertise, and tacit expertise is a wasting asset because its holders are retiring. A royalty share turns those workers from data laborers into stakeholders, which is a legal, ethical and recruiting advantage the $3-an-hour vendors cannot copy.
first_30_days: Recruit 15 retired electricians and pipefitters via IBEW and UA retiree halls and local Facebook groups. Get two robotics startups to pre-pay $25-50k each for 100 hours. Equip people with a $400 kit and a one-page site consent and PII-blur workflow. Deliver the first 20 hours with narration and get a written reference from each buyer.

title: Restaurant Kitchens as Chefs for Small Care Homes
one_liner: License a turnkey program that lets restaurants use dead hours to cook dietitian-approved, texture-modified meals for 6-20 bed assisted-living and adult-family homes that big foodservice ignores.
customer: Operators of small licensed residential care homes (adult family homes, board-and-care, personal care homes, small RCFEs) pay per resident per day, typically $8-12 for lunch and dinner. Adult children pay for premium 'chef-cooked' upgrades. The restaurant is the supplier, and the platform takes a license fee and revenue share.
problem: In a small care home, food is the main daily pleasure and the top resident complaint, yet it is cooked by overworked caregivers from warehouse-club and broadline food, with little variety and hard-to-manage special diets (mechanical soft, pureed, low-sodium, diabetic). Sodexo and Compass do not serve 6-bed homes and meals-on-wheels serves people at home. Meanwhile my kitchens sit idle from 2 to 5pm and on slow days, my cooks want more hours, and my dine-in traffic is soft.
solution: A meal program in a box for restaurants: a rotating 5-week menu library with dietitian sign-off and texture-modified variants (IDDSI levels), allergen and diet labels, batch-cook and cook-chill (or same-day hot delivery) SOPs, a state-specific health-department pre-clearance checklist and HACCP plan templates, routing and billing software, and a contracted registered dietitian on retainer. The restaurant cooks in dead hours and delivers 2-3 times a week in labeled pans, and the care home reheats. Ten homes at about $17-22k per year each is $170-220k of found revenue at healthy contribution margin on capacity that was previously idle.
why_now: The 65+ population is growing fast (the 'Peak 65' wave runs through about 2027). Families are shifting to small, cheaper residential homes rather than large assisted-living campuses. Restaurant dine-in traffic has been soft and owners are actively looking for non-traffic revenue. Kitchen labor is short, and steady off-peak hours help retention. Public state license lists make the small-home buyer easy to find. I couldn't verify current home counts this session, so pull the licensing-list counts state by state before building.
revenue_model: Onboarding fee of $1-2k per restaurant, plus 10-15% of meal revenue, plus software billing at about $100 per month per restaurant. Optional premium tier for adult-child paid 'chef upgrades' and dietitian services.
non_obvious_insight: The gold is in the mismatch between an idle asset and an ignored customer. Small-home operators are often immigrant nurses and caregivers running a tiny business with no procurement power, and no large foodservice company will serve them, but a two-location restaurant can absorb a 300-meal-per-week route into dead hours at nearly zero marginal labor cost. What a restaurant cannot do alone is the compliance layer (texture modification, diet labeling, dietitian review, regulator pre-clearance), and that is the product.
first_30_days: Pull the state's public list of small residential care homes and shortlist 30 within a 15-minute drive. Call my health department to confirm what is required to supply prepared meals from a licensed restaurant to a licensed facility. Hire a freelance registered dietitian by the hour for one 2-week menu. Offer 3 homes a free trial week, then convert them at about $9 per resident per day. Document the SOPs and the regulator's answer as the first version of the product.

title: City Micro-Rule API for Group Tour Operators
one_liner: A continuously updated database of group caps, loudspeaker rules, coach drop-off bans, fees and overnight-parking bans across overtouristed places, delivered as an itinerary checker for tour operators and campervan renters.
customer: Small and mid-size group tour operators, DMCs, shore-excursion companies, guide associations and campervan or RV rental firms in Europe.
problem: Cities answer overtourism with many small rules, such as group-size caps and loudspeaker bans in places like Venice and Amsterdam, plus coach access fees and wild-camping bans elsewhere. These live in local-language ordinances, and fines fall on operators and guides. Nobody publishes a single source of truth.
solution: Use multilingual LLM ingestion of municipal ordinances with human legal review for the top 60 cities. The product is an itinerary checker that flags violations and fees, a weekly change digest, an API for booking systems and a WhatsApp bot for guides.
why_now: Municipal crackdowns keep multiplying (Barcelona, Palma, Venice, Amsterdam, the Balearics, Glasgow's levy from Jan 2027). Long-context LLMs make parsing ordinances in many languages cheap only recently.
revenue_model: USD 79-299 per month per operator, enterprise API licences for cruise lines and campervan renters, and paid city packs.
non_obvious_insight: Overtourism policy has fragmented into thousands of tiny local rules. The pain is compliance risk rather than any single rule, and every new rule makes the product more valuable.
first_30_days: Curate rules for 10 cities (for example Venice, Rome, Florence, Amsterdam, Barcelona, Dubrovnik, Lisbon, Athens, Edinburgh and Kyoto) with local guides. Sell 10 operators at USD 99 per month through guide associations, and publish free rules-by-city pages for SEO lead generation.

title: Jobs-per-Megawatt Factory Recruiting for Public Power
one_liner: Represent municipal electric utilities in recruiting manufacturers by packaging spare feeder capacity, in-hand transformers and industrial rates into a 'jobs per megawatt' pitch that data centers cannot match.
customer: Municipal and public-power utilities and city economic-development agencies (retainer of roughly $3-6k a month). Manufacturers pay a success fee later.
problem: Data centers are absorbing grid capacity, and transformer and switchgear prices are up 89-96% since 2019. Factory construction is down 22-32% from peak while nondefense capital-goods orders hit a record $85.9B, so reshoring is happening as retrofits that need power upgrades, not as new shells. Interconnection at investor-owned utilities takes years, and site selectors rarely look at small public utilities.
solution: A 'Load-Readiness Dossier' per feeder or substation: available megawatts, transformer status and lead times, industrial rate schedules, demand-charge modeling and permitting path. Match it to manufacturers with announced expansions (tariff-motivated onshoring, USMCA re-routers, foundries and magnet or metal processors) and to site selectors. Add a shared transformer reserve pool for small municipal utilities and help negotiate long-term service commitments.
why_now: Data-center demand collided with the reshoring wave in 2026. Section 232 tiers reward US-melted metals and full-value duties are pushing firms to add domestic capacity, and the machinery tier's 15% relief runs through 2027. Utilities are being asked to make loads decisions faster than most can handle.
revenue_model: $3-6k a month retainer per utility, a success fee per megawatt or per signed customer (paid by the manufacturer or shared), and optional financing of pre-bought transformer inventory.
non_obvious_insight: A public utility's incentives are the reverse of an investor-owned utility's. A 5 MW machining plant with hundreds of jobs beats a 100 MW data center with a few dozen jobs for a city council and for spreading fixed costs, yet no one markets to these utilities. Transformer-in-hand is the strongest closing argument.
first_30_days: Select 10 public-power utilities in manufacturing states (Ohio, Indiana, Tennessee, Texas, the Carolinas) and build dossiers from public tariffs, EIA data and integrated resource plans. Pitch 3 economic-development agencies and sign two paid pilot retainers.

title: Costly-Commitment Kits for Fitness Congregations
one_liner: A retention product for boutique gyms and run clubs that borrows religion's real community mechanism, costly commitment, to turn members into a congregation.
customer: Owners of boutique fitness studios, CrossFit boxes, climbing gyms and multi-site run clubs, with franchisors as the scale channel.
problem: Gen Z made up 47% of new gym joins in 2025 yet posts the highest churn (around 54% in one industry dataset), and nearly half of them say community is why they stay. Studios respond with discounts, apps and easier joining, which attracts free-riders and does not build attachment.
solution: A kit of printed rites, a coach's liturgy guide and light software: an initiation for a founding cohort, attendance vows made to a partner, earned 'colors' for milestones, a dawn 'vigil' class, rites for return-from-injury and for a member's death, and a warm leaving ritual. We A/B the kit across studios against controls on 90-day retention.
why_now: ABC Fitness's 2025 year-end report shows Gen Z dominating new joins and community as a top reason to stay. Run clubs and studios are already positioned as a substitute for church, and retention is the KPI that owners pay to move.
revenue_model: $199-499 per month per studio for the kit and software, a performance option of about 10% of measured retention gains, and licensing to franchisors across their locations.
non_obvious_insight: The whole industry builds community by removing friction, while religious sociology (Iannaccone's 'Why Strict Churches Are Strong') finds that commitment, sacrifice and visible costs create strong communities and free-rider filters. Add cost that feels like meaning (time, visibility, obligation) instead of a fee and members become attached, so the friction studios fear is the mechanism.
first_30_days: Recruit five studios from one local franchise. Run a founding-cohort covenant for new joiners and compare 90-day retention against control cohorts. Publish the result and pitch it to franchise developers.

title: Ship-Anywhere Prices for Pickup-Only Auction Lots
one_liner: Embed binding, lot-level delivered prices and a booked load-out window into online auction listings, so pickup-only machinery, estate and surplus lots attract national bidders, with the broker taking a cut of freight and the auctioneer sharing the hammer-price uplift.
customer: Regional auctioneers and liquidators selling machine tools, farm and construction equipment, restaurant and commercial surplus, estates and government surplus on HiBid, Proxibid, AuctionZip or their own sites. The buyer pays the freight.
problem: Pickup-only lots limit bidders to roughly a 100-200 mile radius and depress hammer prices. Existing help is an estimate (Proxibid embeds a uShip-based estimator showing approximate costs from comparable moves) or the buyer scrambling after winning, with a 3-7 day storage or removal deadline running. For a broker, pricing a 2,400-lb lathe at a rural site with one forklift and a Thursday-only load-out is a five-minute call. For a buyer it is a week of failed quotes, so out-of-area buyers simply do not bid.
solution: A listing-time tool. The auctioneer enters the pickup address and lot photos, dimensions and weight (a vision model plus a checklist estimates weight and cube from photos). It returns a binding delivered price by buyer ZIP, locked at bid time, including liftgate or loading, crating and a delivery window. On a win, it dispatches to a vetted pool of hot-shot, box truck, flatbed, lowboy and LTL carriers, books a load-out slot with the auction site's forklift operator, and pays carriers quickly. The auctioneer sees an A/B report of bidders per lot with and without delivered pricing.
why_now: Auction sales have moved largely online, and 2026 platform practice is to spell out freight and special-handling requirements and add approval steps before bidders commit to shipping charges. Vision models can now estimate weight and dimensions from listing photos well enough to quote. Small-load carriers (hot-shot, box truck) are plentiful because the freight market is soft and small carriers need loads.
revenue_model: 15-25% gross margin on freight, since small specialty loads carry higher broker margins than truckload. Typical freight ticket is $400-$1,800. Optionally share 5% of freight with the auctioneer, and later charge a per-lot fee tied to verified hammer-price uplift.
non_obvious_insight: The auctioneer's real problem is not shipping, it is bidder radius. Buyers do not bid on what they cannot price, so quote friction, not freight cost, kills out-of-area bids, which makes pre-bid freight pricing a hammer-price lever that can pay for itself. Also, the binding constraint at rural sites is the single forklift and a narrow load-out window, which no marketplace models. Solve that and carriers love the load because dwell is short.
first_30_days: Sign 5 auctioneers with many pickup-only lots. Concierge-price 50 lots by hand (form plus broker phone calls) and add a 'delivered to your ZIP' link in the lot description. Compare unique bidders and hammer price against matched control lots. Ship 40 lots under existing brokerage authority, and collect the freight margin only. Test estate sales and government surplus as second segments.

title: Fry-Oil Co-op Escaping Evergreen Renderer Contracts
one_liner: Aggregate independent restaurants' used cooking oil, sell it to biofuel buyers at market with sensor-verified traceability, and hand the owner the check the big renderer keeps.
customer: Independent restaurants and small chains with 2-20 fryer-heavy units are the supply side and pay no fee. Local independent oil collectors, biodiesel, renewable diesel and SAF feedstock processors and brokers are the demand side and pay the co-op. Revenue is the spread plus a small sensor rental fee.
problem: Used fry oil is a commodity that biofuel makers have been bidding up, yet independents are locked into 3-year auto-renewing pickup contracts with a large renderer or bin company. The restaurant is paid a pittance or nothing, or is even charged fees. Bins overflow, which brings health-code and odor problems. Thieves steal oil at night, and nobody reconciles what the oil is actually worth. Owners don't switch because the termination window is a 60-90 day certified-letter deadline buried in the contract, and nobody has time to run a bid.
solution: A co-op platform that: (1) tracks each member's contract renewal date and files the non-renewal notice on time; (2) runs a monthly reverse auction among local collectors so that volume, not the restaurant, gets the price; (3) installs a roughly $40 ultrasonic fill sensor and a lockable tank cap, so pickups trigger at 80% full and every pickup is photo- or QR-verified; (4) issues a statement per pickup indexed to a published used-cooking-oil price series; and (5) produces per-restaurant chain-of-custody records that renewable-fuel producers need to prove domestic, traceable feedstock.
why_now: As I understand it, federal clean-fuel incentives (45Z) now favor North American feedstock, and concern about mislabeled imported used oil has raised the value of traceable domestic oil. Renewable diesel and SAF capacity keeps growing. Cheap cellular fill sensors are widely available. Restaurants' margins are so thin that any found cash gets attention. Verify the current feedstock price index and the 45Z sourcing rules before you pitch.
revenue_model: 20-30% spread on oil sold, indexed and transparent, plus $10-30 per month for the sensor and tank lock. Later add a premium for verified-traceable oil sold to fuel producers, and carbon-intensity documentation fees.
non_obvious_insight: The incumbent's real product is the locked contract and route density, not the oil service, so the way in is the calendar rather than a better price. The contract renewal date is the CRM key: a 90-day-out certified non-renewal letter, filed for the owner, is the growth engine. Owners think they are getting 'free removal', so nobody shops it. Also, per-restaurant traceability is worth more to fuel buyers than the oil's volume alone.
first_30_days: Walk one restaurant row and photograph each bin's contract label, and note the pickup company and renewal date for 40 restaurants in one metro. Sign one local collector or small biodiesel maker as a buyer with a written price index. Enroll 8-10 off-contract or month-to-month members, including my own two locations. Install sensors and lock caps, run the first monthly auction, and show each owner a side-by-side statement of what their old vendor paid versus what the co-op did.

title: Film Camera Repair Guild and Parts Mill
one_liner: A training-plus-parts network that multiplies the number of people able to repair 1970s-90s film cameras, using 3D-printed and machined parts and paid video teardown courses.
customer: Independent repair techs and serious hobbyists (parts kits and courses), used-camera shops and labs (bulk repaired-and-warrantied stock), and consumers via mail-in.
problem: The film revival is real but repairers are retiring (ABC News Dec 2025; PetaPixel Jan 2026), many now refuse to service certain models, and mechanical parts are hard to source. Dead cameras mean lost film buyers.
solution: Start with the ~25 most popular bodies (AE-1, K1000, X-700, FM2 and similar). Sell light-seal, mirror-bumper and foam kits plus printed or CNC-machined gears. Publish paid step-by-step repair courses, certify guild repairers, route overflow mail-in jobs to them, and sell warrantied repaired stock wholesale to used shops.
why_now: The retirement wave is now documented in mainstream press. Cheap multi-material printing and on-demand metal parts vendors exist. Film demand keeps rising among under-35s, and used-camera prices are climbing.
revenue_model: Parts kits ($8-40), course subscriptions (~$20/month), a ~25% share of routed repairs, and wholesale of repaired cameras with warranty.
non_obvious_insight: Film-industry insiders assume the constraint on the revival is film stock and new cameras. It is repair capacity: repair knowledge is tacit and walking out the door. Apprenticeship packaged as content, plus a parts supply, is the picks-and-shovels play, and every dead SLR is a lost film customer.
first_30_days: Buy 20 broken AE-1 and K1000 lots on eBay and film every teardown. Sell foam and seal kits on Etsy and eBay with instructions. Pre-sell 100 lifetime course seats to r/AnalogCommunity. Recruit 3 retiring techs as paid instructors on revenue share.

title: Deorphanization Factory for AI-Nominated Enzymes
one_liner: A pooled-substrate, NGS-readout assay line that assigns function to hundreds of AI-nominated unknown enzymes per week for hundreds of dollars each.
customer: Genome-editing and enzyme-discovery companies, frontier-lab and academic agent-discovery teams, and industrial enzyme groups.
problem: Agent swarms nominate candidates far faster than anyone can characterize them. Anthropic's run went from 200,000+ reverse transcriptases to 20 candidates in 21 hours, yet the function of the resulting array-associated reverse transcriptase (ART) system is still unknown, with human validation and biochemical characterization as the bottleneck.
solution: Cell-free expression of candidates in 384-well format. Universal substrate panels of pooled, barcoded DNA and RNA oligo libraries are incubated with each enzyme. NGS reads out cutting, copying, ligating and editing, producing an automated activity 'passport' (substrate preferences, cofactors, temperature). Start with nucleic-acid-acting enzymes (nucleases, RTs, recombinases, ligases) where pooled NGS readout works, and add mass-spec panels for small-molecule enzymes later.
why_now: Anthropic's Sept 2026 ART discovery came with an explicit invitation to partner with other scientists. DNA synthesis is cheap, cell-free expression is mature, and agent discovery volumes are exploding.
revenue_model: $300-1,000 per enzyme passport, $50-250k discovery-partnership programs, and shared upside on licensed hits.
non_obvious_insight: Compute is commoditizing discovery, so the scarce step is cheap, standardized characterization. Pooled assays turn function into a read instead of a project. A passport format could become the exchange currency between agent discoverers and enzyme users.
first_30_days: Build a v0 pooled-substrate library and assay for reverse transcriptases and nucleases. Characterize 50 public candidates and publish the results. Approach 5 editing-tool companies and 3 academic agent-discovery groups with a $10k 50-enzyme pilot.

title: Funeral Home Land-and-Business Split Advisory
one_liner: An advisor that separates aging independent funeral directors' real estate from their operating business. The land goes to housing developers, the shrunken business is leased back or sold to a consolidator, and the advisor earns fees and a small equity slice.
customer: Owners of independent funeral homes (about 75% of 15,401 US funeral homes are family or privately owned), especially those over 60 without a successor. Infill housing developers and investors buy the land. Consolidators such as SCI and Everstory may buy the business.
problem: These sites were built for burial-era visitation: large buildings with big parking lots on prime corridors. With cremation at about 63%, flat deaths and volume down 1.4% at SCI, the buildings are oversized while taxes and upkeep rise. Owners get lowball offers for the business that bundle the land. Developers never see these parcels, which are off-market and not listed. The business buyer pool and the land buyer pool are disjoint and do not talk to each other.
solution: Screen parcels using zoning, lot size, transit and local cremation share, plus state licensing data on owner age. Offer owners a split: sell or ground-lease the land to a developer and lease back a compact 2,500-3,000 sf service footprint (or a ground-floor space in the new mixed-use building), or sell the business alone to a consolidator. Package parcels for states with single-staircase and missing-middle reforms. Sell paid feasibility studies first, then take closing fees and equity.
why_now: Single-staircase reform (7 states in 2025, Michigan in July 2026) and California AB 2074 lower infill costs. Rates near 7.5% make greenfield harder, so infill parcels gain appeal. Consolidator cash flow is strong (SCI operating cash flow up 43%), which makes them acquisitive. Cremation growth is making the buildings redundant.
revenue_model: $5-10K paid feasibility studies, a 2-3% success fee on the land transaction, 5-10% carried equity in the project, and a fee when the business is sold to a consolidator.
non_obvious_insight: Funeral homes are a large class of buildings whose function shrank while owners still think of them as businesses, not real estate. The highest and best use is often housing, and the key is to split the land from the operation so neither buyer pool discounts the other.
first_30_days: Pull funeral home parcels in two or three states with recent zoning reform. Contact 100 owners aged 60 or over (from state funeral-board license data). Sign three paid feasibility studies. Partner with one infill developer and one consolidator to test appetite.

title: Tariff Surcharge Clawback for Downstream Payers
one_liner: Recover itemized tariff surcharges from suppliers who were refunded the tariffs, on contingency, and give surcharge-collecting firms a defensive ledger.
customer: Small contractors, restaurants, repair shops and retailers who were invoiced a separate 'tariff surcharge' line by suppliers in 2025-26, plus small firms that added such surcharges to their own customers' bills.
problem: SCOTUS ruled on 2026-02-20 that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, and about $166B in CBP refunds go to the importer of record (about $81B paid by July). Over 40% of small firms saw tariff cost increases and 76% of international sourcers passed them on, so the firm that paid the pass-through gets nothing. Each claim is too small ($200-$8k) for a lawyer, and firms that billed surcharges to their own customers now carry their own exposure.
solution: Read-only scan of the owner's mailbox and QuickBooks/Xero pulls every tariff or surcharge line from vendor invoices and from the firm's own customer invoices. It builds a two-sided surcharge ledger (paid upstream, collected downstream), then generates supplier demand letters that cite the invoice wording and contract terms. Unpaid claims escalate to small-claims templates or a partner attorney. Claims are strongest where the invoice said the surcharge was itemized or refundable. Because one supplier can owe hundreds of customers, settlements can be negotiated per supplier instead of per claim.
why_now: Refunds have been flowing through CBP's automated system since April 2026, so suppliers are holding refund cash right now, before it is absorbed into margins. Invoice records are fresh and 2026 books have not closed.
revenue_model: 25-30% contingency on recovered dollars, with a $49 flat fee for the ledger and audit. Later, a per-supplier settlement-program fee.
non_obvious_insight: Refund law is written for importers, but the money trail is an invoice trail. Itemized invoices are contract evidence, and thousands of tiny claims against a few hundred suppliers form a portfolio no law firm will touch. The same ledger doubles as a defense file for firms that billed surcharges.
first_30_days: Offer a free 'surcharge audit' in trade-specific Facebook groups and subreddits (HVAC, restaurant equipment, apparel resellers). Hand-review 50 mailboxes and find the 10 suppliers with the most itemized surcharges. Retain a consumer-protection attorney to review the demand-letter template, send the first 100 letters, and measure the response rate.

title: Bridge Loans for Medicare Drug-Price Refunds
one_liner: Fund the 3-4 week float independent pharmacies now carry on Medicare's negotiated-price drugs, underwritten on predictable refund data, before Ozempic joins the list in January.
customer: Independent pharmacies with senior-heavy books, especially those serving long-term care, then 5-50 store groups and PSAOs. Average exposure is estimated at over $27,000 a month per community pharmacy.
problem: Since January 1, 2026, pharmacies pay wholesalers full price for Eliquis, Jardiance, Xarelto, Farxiga, Januvia, Entresto and others, dispense at Medicare's Maximum Fair Price, and wait weeks for the difference to arrive through the Medicare Transaction Facilitator. Estimates put the float at $27k+ a month for the average community pharmacy, over $500M a month industry-wide, on top of wholesalers who still auto-debit weekly. On thin margins that is a real solvency risk. Banks see a pharmacy, not an insured refund.
solution: Start with a reconciliation tool that ingests the pharmacy's PMS claims export and the MTF remittance files and shows late or missing refunds. Then offer a non-recourse advance of about 90% of the expected refund on each week's MFP claims, repaid from the actual MTF payment through a controlled deposit account or sweep. Confirm with CMS and the facilitator what payment-routing options exist, and fall back to a bank-account sweep if third-party routing is not allowed.
why_now: The program only became real on January 1, 2026, and it is already causing cash-flow warnings from pharmacy coalitions. On January 1, 2027, 15 more drugs join, including semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy, Rybelsus), which multiplies the float. Wholesalers have not yet solved it and the bank market does not understand it, so there is a window of a few quarters before someone standardizes the answer.
revenue_model: A fee of about 1-1.75% per advance cycle, which works out to roughly 15-25% annualized, plus a $99 a month reconciliation subscription. Contingency of about 10% on missing refunds recovered. Later, sell or syndicate the receivables to a credit fund.
non_obvious_insight: To a bank this looks like distress lending to a struggling small business. In reality it is close to prime paper: the obligor is a drug manufacturer with a statutory duty to pay, routed through a federal facilitator, backed by claim-level data. Only someone who knows how PMS claims map to MFP eligibility, and how a reversal or dispute can claw a refund back, can underwrite it. The free reconciliation report is the wedge that gets the data before any money goes out.
first_30_days: Offer a free 'find my missing refunds' report to 25 pharmacies through state association newsletters and pharmacy owner Facebook groups. Line up a $500k credit line from a regional bank or family office and keep the first ten advances small. Talk to a fintech attorney about commercial-financing disclosure laws by state. Approach one PSAO about distribution.

title: Parametric Insurance on Colorado River Shortage
one_liner: Insurance and hedges that pay out when official Colorado River operating triggers or reservoir projections cross agreed thresholds, sold to large industrial and municipal water buyers.
customer: Chip fabs, data centers, breweries, resorts, master-planned developers and municipal utilities that depend on Lower Basin supplies. Buyers pay premiums, and reinsurance and capital-markets funds take the risk.
problem: Powell plus Mead storage is about 36% and 95% of the basin is in drought. About $1.4T of annual activity is exposed, yet businesses cannot hedge water-supply or rate shocks except by capex. Until this year the rules were too ambiguous to write a contract against.
solution: Start with a Lower Basin water-supply risk index and term sheets, sold to muni-bond investors and industrial water buyers. Then build a parametric product that pays on published operating triggers or reservoir projections, funded through a surplus-lines or Lloyd's partner with an experienced weather-risk insurer. Payouts fund contingency supply, recycling or trucked water.
why_now: The Aug 2026 Record of Decision set the 2027-2036 operating framework, converting political ambiguity into published rules that a contract can reference. Capital-markets investors seek risks uncorrelated with catastrophe.
revenue_model: Premium (a percentage of limit), analytics licensing before any policy is issued, and a share of fund fees.
non_obvious_insight: The ROD makes the river's rules legible, which is the precondition for a derivative. The correlated hydrology scares traditional insurers, but that is exactly what non-catastrophe capital wants to hold.
first_30_days: Build the risk index from Reclamation's public 24-Month Study projections and reservoir data. Interview 10 fab, data-center and utility water managers on what loss they fear. Approach one weather-risk reinsurer and one ILS fund. First revenue comes from analytics sold to bond funds and industrial users.

title: Golden-Hour Payment Recall Desk for Small Firms
one_liner: A 24/7 retainer that runs the first 60 minutes after a fraudulent payment: bank fraud desks, recall requests and freeze filings, using a pre-built bank contact book.
customer: SMBs with 5-250 employees, sold through bookkeepers, CPAs, MSPs and crime-insurance brokers, at $99-299 per month. Insurers can subsidize.
problem: The FBI fund-freeze process handled 3,900 incidents ($1.16B attempted) and froze $679M, or 58%, yet individuals and SMBs rarely use it. BEC cost $3.05B and tech-support and takeover fraud $2.13B. One account takeover can fire 50+ ACH transfers to multiple banks, and victims lose the first hours to phone trees and confusion.
solution: At onboarding, capture bank fraud contacts and payment approvers. At incident time, a hotline and web intake runs the playbook: generate the IC3 complaint with the right fields, send correctly formatted ACH return and wire recall requests to sending and receiving banks, escalate to receiving-bank fraud teams, and assemble an evidence and insurance packet. Track which banks respond fastest.
why_now: IC3's 2025 report is the first to show freeze rates clearly, and instant rails have shrunk the window. Takeover cases are rising and shifting away from classic BEC.
revenue_model: Monthly retainer, $500-2,500 per incident, and insurer funding.
non_obvious_insight: The money is not gone in 24 hours: 58% of attempted funds froze when the process was used. The constraint is speed and paperwork, which is a service business. The moat is the bank response-time dataset that banks do not publish.
first_30_days: Sign 10 bookkeeping and MSP partners. Write the runbook and directory of top-50 bank fraud lines and 200 credit unions. Staff with two part-time ex-bank fraud analysts on rotation and pilot at $99 per month.

title: Verified-Real Dating Portraits Shot by Wedding Photographers
one_liner: A consumer brand that rents wedding photographers' dead winter months to shoot candid-directed dating and profile portraits, delivered with a signed 'real photo' certificate.
customer: Single adults aged 25-45 in the top 20 US metros paying $179-299 per session. Secondary channel: matchmakers and dating coaches buying sessions for their clients.
problem: Wedding photographers earn most of their income in a compressed May-October window and sit mostly idle from November to March, with skills and gear already paid for. Meanwhile dating profiles are flooded with AI-generated and heavily retouched photos, so users and matches increasingly distrust every photo. Existing options are cheap AI headshot apps (the very thing everyone distrusts), generic corporate headshot studios that make stiff LinkedIn photos, and a few dating-photo studios with model-y aesthetics. Nobody is selling authenticity as a verifiable, human-shot product.
solution: A productized 60-minute walk-and-talk shoot across three locations using wedding-style directing prompts ('walk toward me and tell me the worst first date you've had') that get natural laughter from stiff people in about 90 seconds. Delivery is 15 edited photos in 48 hours following a dating shot list (full-body, hobby, social proof, pet, non-selfie smile). Each set ships with a 'Real Photo Certificate': Content Credentials (C2PA) from supported cameras, a no-generative-AI editing policy, and a public verification page users can link in their bio. Supply comes from wedding photographers trained in a 90-minute module. The platform handles booking, payment, brand, marketing and QC and keeps 30-35%.
why_now: AI-generated profile photos are now common enough that dating apps have leaned on photo and face verification. Several major camera makers now ship Content Credentials support in newer bodies or firmware, so provenance is technically feasible for small studios. Wedding photographers are also under margin pressure as couples trim coverage hours and guest counts, so winter income is increasingly attractive. 2026 is the first year 'proof a human made this' has real consumer value.
revenue_model: $199-299 per session with a 30-35% platform take. Upsells include a $39 'profile audit' and a re-shoot at 6 months. B2B2C packages for matchmakers and dating coaches at $150 per client.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce skill isn't lighting, it's getting a stiff stranger to laugh convincingly on cue, which wedding photographers do 40 times a summer. The photographer's marginal cost in January is close to zero, so supply arrives almost free while every competitor pays full-time studio rents.
first_30_days: Pick one metro and recruit 6 wedding photographers who complain publicly about winter. Run 20 pilot shoots at a $99 launch price, sourced from local Instagram/Reddit dating communities, run clubs and singles events, and from 5 matchmakers and dating coaches. Ask each client for before/after match counts (self-reported) and permission to publish testimonials. Register a public verification page for each set. Charge full price from shoot 21 onward.

title: Youth Clubs as the Ban-Proof Group Chat
one_liner: A roster-anchored messaging layer for sports leagues, scout councils and youth groups that reuses the club's adult-verified roster as a safe, auditable chat for 9-15 year olds, paid by the club.
customer: Regional youth sports leagues, scout councils, robotics/FIRST teams and church youth groups (5k-100k members), plus their liability insurers. Parents use it free.
problem: Under-16 bans (Australia, Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, several US states) push kids into private chats and games. Everyone's answer is a new 'safe social network for kids', which dies on cold start. Meanwhile clubs already hold the verified network (background-checked coaches, rosters, parent contacts) but run it on WhatsApp, GroupMe and Snap groups with coach-to-child DMs. Youth-safety policies such as SafeSport's (from memory) prohibit exactly those DMs, and leagues cannot audit them.
solution: Team and league chats built on the registration data the club already has (DOB, parent identity). No one-to-one adult-minor DMs unless a second guardian is copied. Kid accounts are age-tiered and parent-linked, with no discovery, ads or strangers. Keyword flags go to the club safety officer. An exportable audit log goes to the insurer. Kids age out into open platforms at 16.
why_now: Ban leakage (VPNs under A$20 a month, 75% of Australian teens planning to stay on) means kids need somewhere else to talk. Insurers are tightening abuse-and-molestation coverage (from memory). Fall registration season is happening now, so the product can ride the season's registration fee.
revenue_model: $1-4 per member per season, bundled into the league's registration fee. Enterprise licence for councils. Referral fees or premium credits from insurers.
non_obvious_insight: The hard part of safe kids' social is distribution and verification, not software. A club has the graph, the identity check, a legal duty of care and a budget, and nobody has packaged that.
first_30_days: Interview 15 league directors and two youth-sports insurers. Ship a white-label chat on Stream or Sendbird for two leagues in one metro. Sell it as 'audit-ready coach-athlete messaging' at $1 per kid during fall registration. Collect an insurer endorsement or premium-credit letter.
